sentences.text: Reports described that good data is essential for delivering cancer care, as good data equals better care, which results in better health in communities and provinces.
Cancer registry data comes from multiple sources including pathology reports, histology reports, autopsy reports, diagnostic laboratory information, and vital statistics.
The Ontario Cancer Registry tracked cancer incidence over a twenty-year period from 1964-1983.
Provincial cancer registries collect data from a variety of sources and direct activities toward addressing issues of data accuracy, completeness, and integrity.

The Nova Scotia Cancer Registry contains information on all Nova Scotians diagnosed with cancer and is used to produce descriptive cancer statistics, support cancer epidemiology work, and approved research.
The Nova Scotia Cancer Registry includes basic demographic information, disease information such as diagnosis date and disease stage, mortality data, and primary cancer treatment data.

The Alberta Cancer Registry records and maintains data on all new primary cancers and cancer deaths occurring in the province and captures all invasive and in situ cancers diagnosed amongst Albertans.
The Alberta Cancer Registry learns of new cancers from pathology reports sent by laboratories throughout the province, operative reports, discharge summaries, x-ray reports, and autopsy reports.

The New Brunswick Cancer Registry provides information on cancer incidence and mortality distributions, trends in cancer incidence and mortality, relative survival estimates for various cancers, and future projections on cancer incidence and mortality.

The Prince Edward Island Provincial Tumor Registry provides cancer incidence data to Statistics Canada from sources including pathology reports and a monthly list of cancer deaths from Vital Statistics.
